files.lesson.md: --- order: 23 unit: solve10 node: AC9M10A02 n1 assumes: [AC9M8A02 n3] # Year 8 Inequalities: solving, reversing for a negative, rays connection: ride-budget title: Solving inequalities summary: "Solve an inequality from a budget, read the answer in the context (whole rides, not 6.2), reverse the sign when you divide by a negative, put the unknown on both sides and solve a range." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "A fair has an entry fee and a price for each ride, and your money is fixed. How do you work out the most rides you can go on?" app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8372 url: http://127.0.0.1:8372/index.html readySelector: "#sl-r" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: inequality.yml#explain-pic, caption: "$12 + 4.5r$ against the $40 limit: 6 rides cost $39, and 7 would cost $43.50." } explainClip: query: { code: "@inequality.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "Rides until the cost passes $40" say: "Add rides until the cost passes forty dollars." clip: - caption: { text: "No rides: just the $12 entry.", say: "With no rides, you have paid the twelve dollar entry." } - wait: 900 - caption: { text: "Each ride adds $4.50. Keep going while the point is below the dashed $40 line.", say: "Each ride adds four dollars fifty. Keep going while the point is under the line." } - click: Make r bigger - click: Make r bigger - click: Make r bigger - click: Make r bigger - click: Make r bigger - click: Make r bigger - wait: 700 - caption: { text: "6 rides: $39. One more ride goes over.", say: "Six rides cost thirty nine dollars. One more goes over." } - click: Make r bigger - wait: 1400 --- Last year you solved inequalities like equations and reversed the sign for a negative. This lesson puts them in a budget, where the answer has to make sense as well as be right. (All prices here are made up.) ## Predict: the rides ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to the number of rides shows who forgets the entry fee (40 ÷ 4.50 is about 8.9) and who rounds up." check: type: predict q: "Entry is $12 and each ride is $4.50. You have $40. What is the most rides you can go on?" options: - "$6$" - "$7$" - "$8$" - "$9$" actual: "6. After the $12 entry you have $28, and 28 ÷ 4.50 is about 6.2, so 6 whole rides. 8 forgets the entry fee (40 ÷ 4.50 is 8.9). 7 rounds 6.2 up, but 7 rides cost 12 + 31.50 = $43.50, which is over." ``` Make a guess, then test it on the board. ## Run: add rides ```step stage: run insight: "The cost is 12 + 4.5 per ride, and the most rides is the last whole number where the cost is still at most 40: the inequality is 12 + 4.5r ≤ 40." try: { playground: board, starter: "inequality.yml#run", height: 560 } check: { type: board, text: "Move $r$ to the most rides that keep the point on or under the dashed $40 line. Was your prediction right?", when: "r = 6" } ``` $r$ is the number of rides. The slanted line is the cost, and the dashed line is your $40. ## Investigate: solve, then read it ```step stage: investigate insight: "Solving 12 + 4.5r ≤ 40 gives r ≤ 6.2, and the context decides the answer: rides come whole, so 6. Lena divides by a negative and keeps the sign, and her check fails." try: { playground: board, starter: "inequality.yml#ray", height: 380 } tasks: - starter: "inequality.yml#ray" hint: ["Take 6 from both sides, then divide by 2.5.", "8 hours costs exactly $26, which you can afford: closed circle."] check: { type: board, text: "A scooter costs $6 to hire and $2.50 an hour, and you have $26. Solve $6 + 2.5x \\le 26$, then show it: move $P$, choose the circle and the direction.", when: "x(P) = 8 and k = 1 and s = -1", explain: "2.5x ≤ 20, so x ≤ 8: a closed circle at 8 (8 hours costs exactly $26), shaded left." } - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#lena" text: "Lena solves $40 - 4.5r \\ge 12$, the money left after the rides. Click the line where her working goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: inequality-reverse explain: "Line 3: dividing by −4.5 reverses the sign, so r ≤ 6.2. Her check on line 4 is the clue: r = 0 is allowed, and 0 ≥ 6.2 is false." - check: type: question q: "$12 + 4.5r \\le 40$ gives $r \\le 6.2$. How many rides can you go on?" options: ["6", "7", "6.2"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "7 rides cost 12 + 31.50 = $43.50, which is over $40.", "Rides come whole: you can't go on 0.2 of a ride."] explain: "r ≤ 6.2 includes 6 but not 7, and rides are whole numbers, so 6 is the most. The solution of the inequality is a range, and the context picks the values that make sense." ``` ### Solve and show it Here's how a budget becomes an inequality. ```worked 9 + 3.5h \le 30 :: $9 to hire a bike plus $3.50 an hour, and no more than $30. 3.5h \le 21 :: Take 9 from both sides. h \le 6 :: Divide by 3.5 (positive): the sign stays. \text{closed circle at } 6,\ \text{shaded left} :: 6 hours costs exactly $30, which is allowed, so the circle is closed. 9 + 3.5 \times 5 = 26.50 \le 30 :: Check a value from the shaded part in the original. ``` Now try one on paper, step by step like the example: the scooter, then show it on the board. ### Find the mistake Read Lena's working. Her check is a clue. ### Read the answer ## Modify: one change at a time ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: a negative in front of the unknown, the unknown on both sides, a strict inequality with a whole-number boundary, and a range between two values." try: { playground: board, starter: "inequality.yml#ray", height: 380 } tasks: - starter: "inequality.yml#ray" hint: ["Take 18 from both sides: −3x > −12.", "Divide by −3 and reverse the sign."] check: { type: board, text: "You have $18 and each game costs $3, and you want more than $6 left: $18 - 3x > 6$. Solve it and show it.", when: "x(P) = 4 and k = 0 and s = -1", explain: "−3x > −12, then divide by −3 and reverse: x < 4. Open circle at 4, shaded left. Check x = 3: 18 − 9 = 9 > 6. ✓" } smaller: check: type: question q: "$-3x > -12$. Divide both sides by $-3$. What is the answer?" options: ["$x < 4$", "$x > 4$"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Dividing by a negative reverses the sign."] explain: "Dividing by −3 reverses > into <: x < 4." - starter: "inequality.yml#ray" hint: ["Take 2x from both sides first.", "3x + 3 ≥ 15, then 3x ≥ 12."] check: { type: board, text: "The unknown is on both sides. Solve $5x + 3 \\ge 2x + 15$ and show it.", when: "x(P) = 4 and k = 1 and s = 1", explain: "3x + 3 ≥ 15, 3x ≥ 12, x ≥ 4: closed circle at 4, shaded right." } - hint: ["$12 + 4.5r < 39$ gives $4.5r < 27$.", "Is 6 less than 6, or equal to it?"] check: type: number q: "Edge case: you have to spend less than $39, so $12 + 4.5r < 39$. What is the most whole rides?" answer: 5 feedback: - [6, "6 rides cost exactly $39, but the sign is strict: it has to be less than 39."] explain: "4.5r < 27, so r < 6. The boundary 6 is not included, so the most whole rides is 5." - hint: ["Do the same to all three parts.", "Add 4 to all three, then divide all three by 2."] check: type: question q: "Solve $8 < 2x - 4 \\le 14$." options: ["$6 < x \\le 9$", "$4 < x \\le 7$", "$6 \\le x < 9$", "$12 < x \\le 18$"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Add 4 to all three parts, not take it away: 12 < 2x ≤ 18.", "The circles are the other way: the left sign is < (open) and the right is ≤ (closed).", "That is 12 < 2x ≤ 18. Divide all three by 2."] explain: "Add 4: 12 < 2x ≤ 18. Divide by 2: 6 < x ≤ 9. Open circle at 6, closed at 9." ``` ### A negative ### Both sides ### A strict boundary ### A range ## Practise: solve and read ```step stage: practise insight: "Solving with and without reversal, reading the context, and a range of answers, with the review keeping reshaping fresh." try: { playground: board, starter: "inequality.yml#ray", height: 380 } tasks: - starter: "inequality.yml#ray" check: { type: board, text: "Solve $7 + 3x < 22$ and show it.", when: "x(P) = 5 and k = 0 and s = -1", explain: "3x < 15, x < 5: open circle at 5, shaded left." } - starter: "inequality.yml#ray" check: { type: board, text: "Solve $20 - 2x \\le 8$ and show it.", when: "x(P) = 6 and k = 1 and s = 1", explain: "−2x ≤ −12, then divide by −2 and reverse: x ≥ 6. Closed circle at 6, shaded right." } smaller: check: type: question q: "After taking 20 from both sides, $-2x \\le -12$. What do you do next?" options: ["Divide by −2 and reverse the sign", "Divide by −2 and keep the sign", "Divide by 2 and keep the sign"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Dividing by a negative reverses the sign.", "The −2 is negative: divide by −2, not 2."] explain: "Divide by −2 and reverse: x ≥ 6." - check: type: number q: "A skate park charges $8 entry and $2.50 a game. You have $30. What is the most whole games?" answer: 8 feedback: - [9, "9 games cost 8 + 22.50 = $30.50, which is over."] - [8.8, "Games come whole. 8.8 isn't a number of games."] explain: "8 + 2.5g ≤ 30, so 2.5g ≤ 22 and g ≤ 8.8. The most whole games is 8." - check: type: question q: "Solve $5 - 2x \\ge 11$." options: ["$x \\le -3$", "$x \\ge -3$", "$x \\ge 3$", "$x \\le 3$"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Dividing by −2 reverses the sign.", "5 − 11 is −6, not +6, and then reverse the sign.", "Take 5 from both sides: −2x ≥ 6, so x ≤ −3."] explain: "−2x ≥ 6, then divide by −2 and reverse: x ≤ −3. Check x = −4: 5 + 8 = 13 ≥ 11. ✓" - check: type: number q: "Review: solve $x^2 + x = 20$. Give the positive solution." answer: 4 feedback: - [20, "Move the 20 across first: x² + x − 20 = 0."] - [-5, "That is the other solution. The question asks for the positive one."] explain: "x² + x − 20 = 0, so (x + 5)(x − 4) = 0: x = −5 or x = 4. The positive one is 4." ``` ### Solve and show ### A negative ### In a context ### Reverse or not ### Review Reshaping and factorising, from the last lesson. ## Make: a second park ```step stage: make insight: "Back to the fair: Park B has a higher entry and cheaper rides, so the question is when B costs less, an inequality with the unknown on both sides, read as whole rides." tasks: - hint: ["Park A costs 12 + 4.5r, and Park B costs 20 + 3r.", "Take 12 and 3r from both sides."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "Park B charges $20 entry and $3 a ride. Park A charges $12 entry and $4.50 a ride. Prices are made up. What is the fewest whole rides for which Park B costs less than Park A?" steps: - ["$20 + 3r < 12 + 4.5r$", "Park B costs less than Park A"] - ["$8 < 1.5r$", "take 12 and 3r from both sides"] - ["$r > 5.33\\ldots$", "divide by 1.5 (positive): the sign stays"] - ["$r \\ge 6$", "rides are whole, and 5 is not more than 5.33"] picks: - step: 4 q: "Why is it 6 rides, not 5?" options: ["5 is not more than 5.33, and at 5 rides B ($35) still costs more than A ($34.50)", "5.33 rounds to 5", "6 is the closest whole number to 5.33"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Rounding to the nearest isn't the rule. The inequality is strict: r has to be more than 5.33.", "Closest isn't the rule. The inequality says r > 5.33, so 5 fails and 6 works."] answer: "6" answerLabel: "Fewest rides" feedback: - ["5", "At 5 rides A costs $34.50 and B costs $35. B isn't cheaper yet."] - ["5.33", "Rides come whole: use the first whole number above 5.33."] criteria: - "I wrote both costs and the inequality between them." - "I took the same from both sides and divided by a positive number, so the sign stayed." - "I gave a whole number and checked it in both costs." explain: "r > 5.33, so r ≥ 6. Check at 6 rides: A costs 12 + 27 = $39 and B costs 20 + 18 = $38. B is cheaper." - check: type: number q: "With $40, how many rides can you go on at Park B?" answer: 6 feedback: - [7, "7 rides at B cost 20 + 21 = $41, which is over $40."] - [6.67, "Rides come whole. Round down, not to the nearest."] explain: "20 + 3r ≤ 40, so 3r ≤ 20 and r ≤ 6.67. The most is 6 rides (cost $38), the same as Park A with $40, but B costs $1 less." ``` ### Two parks Do this one on paper first, then type your answer. ### Park B with $40 **Also used in** - **Budgets and limits.** A phone plan with a data cap, or a hire price that includes a fixed fee. - **Comparing plans.** Where one plan becomes cheaper than another is an inequality with the unknown on both sides. - **Next.** Two limits at once: an inequality with two variables, drawn as a shaded region. ```teacher summary: Students solve 12 + 4.5r ≤ 40 for a day at the fair, read r ≤ 6.2 as six whole rides, reverse the sign when dividing by a negative, solve with the unknown on both sides and solve a double inequality; they finish by comparing two parks (AC9M10A02, node 1). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 15 min · Modify 12 min · Practise and Make 10 min goals: - I can solve a linear inequality from a budget and show it on a number line. - I can reverse the sign when I divide by a negative, and say why. - "I can read the answer in the context: whole rides, not 6.2." struggle: Forgetting the entry fee when finding the most rides, rounding to the nearest instead of down, and keeping the sign after dividing by a negative (Lena). Ask students to check a value from their answer in the original before they show it. before: > Do the Run board yourself first. Students need Year 8 Inequalities (solving, reversing for a negative, open and closed circles). This lesson does not teach the reversal again: it uses it in a context where the answer has to make sense, adds the unknown on both sides, a strict inequality with a whole boundary, and a double inequality. The one idea: solve like an equation (reverse for a negative), show the whole range, then ask which values the situation allows. The common mistake is keeping the sign after dividing by a negative (Lena's working, planted after the worked example); her check at r = 0 is the clue. Not a hinge node, but the smaller steps help where students stick: the negative coefficient in Modify and Practise. The number line board shows whole-number and half-number boundaries only, so 6.2 is read from the solved inequality, not placed on the line. All prices (the fair, the bike, the scooter, the skate park, Park A and Park B) are made up for this lesson: no figure here is a real price. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands for 6, 7, 8 and 9. Ask the 8s what they did with the entry fee." - "Run: ask students why the answer is the last whole number under the line, not the nearest." - "Investigate: ask what 6.2 rides would mean, and who would round it up." - "Paper: the try-one after the worked example and the two parks in Make are worked on paper first. Books out, and look for the sign being kept or reversed." - "Modify: before 18 − 3x > 6, ask students to predict whether the ray goes left or right." - "Make: before anyone writes, ask who thinks Park B is cheaper for every number of rides." stuck: - see: A student writes r ≥ 6.2 after dividing by −4.5 (Lena's mistake). ask: Is r = 0 allowed? Does 0 ≥ 6.2 agree? fix: "No: dividing by a negative reverses the sign, so r ≤ 6.2." - see: A student says the most rides is 7. ask: What do 7 rides cost altogether, with the entry? fix: 12 + 31.50 = $43.50, over $40. Round down, not to the nearest. - see: A student gives 6 for 12 + 4.5r < 39. ask: Does 6 rides cost less than $39, or exactly $39? fix: "Exactly $39. The sign is strict, so 6 is not included: 5." stretch: Find when Park B stops being cheaper if its rides were $3.50 instead of $3. Is there a number of rides where they cost the same? Say what the line crossing means. support: "A table of rides 0 to 8 with the cost at each, so students can see the cost cross $40 before they solve. A sentence frame: I have $__ left after the entry, and each ride costs $__, so __ rides." leads: > Continues the Year 10 algebra work (AC9M10A02, node 1). Where it leads: inequalities with two variables and shaded regions (the next node), and linear programming in Year 11 and 12. exit: q: You have $50 and a day costs $14 entry plus $3.50 a ride. What is the most whole rides? a: "10: 14 + 3.5r ≤ 50, so r ≤ 10.28, and 10 whole rides." explain: > An entry of $12 and $4.50 a ride costs $12 + 4.5r$ for $r$ rides. With $40 to spend, $12 + 4.5r \le 40$. Solve it like an equation: $4.5r \le 28$, so $r \le 6.2$. If you divide by a negative, reverse the sign. The solution is a range, but rides come whole, so the context picks the values: the most is 6 rides, which costs $39. Seven would cost $43.50. ```

# Boards for "Solving inequalities" (Year 10). The cost of a day at the fair against the number of rides; then a ray on a number line.

# region: run
widget: graph
x: 0, 10
y: 0, 60
grid: 1, 10
axes: Rides, Cost ($)
slider r: 0, 10, 0
plot: y = 12 + 4.5x
plot: y = 40, dashed
point A: r, 12 + 4.5r
# endregion

# region: explain
widget: graph
x: 0, 10
y: 0, 60
grid: 1, 10
axes: Rides, Cost ($)
slider r: 0, 10, 0
plot: y = 12 + 4.5x
plot: y = 40, dashed
point A: r, 12 + 4.5r
# endregion

# region: explain-pic
widget: graph
x: 0, 10
y: 0, 60
grid: 1, 10
axes: Rides, Cost ($)
plot: y = 12 + 4.5x
plot: y = 40, dashed
point A: 6, 39
# endregion

# region: ray
widget: numberline
range: -6, 12
point P: 0, drag
ray: P
# endregion

# Lena's working for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: lena
Solve 40 − 4.5r ≥ 12.
Take 40 from both sides: −4.5r ≥ −28.
Divide both sides by −4.5: r ≥ 6.2.
Check r = 0: 40 − 0 = 40 ≥ 12 is true, but 0 ≥ 6.2 is false.
# endregion
